channel.title: Pratik Dhanave — Blog
channel.description: Long-form writing on multi-agent AI, medical AI governance, HIPAA-aware architecture, and cloud-native systems.

item.title: Memory in Production — Privacy, Forgetting, Isolation, and Proving It Works
item.description: Production memory is a personal-data system: minimization as selection, answerable 'what do you remember about me', sensitivity tiers, deletion that cascades along provenance edges, hard tenant isolation (memory writes are an injection surface), and layered evals ending in the ablation that proves memory earns its cost. Remembering well is valuable; forgetting well is trustworthy. Closes the series.

item.title: Driving Adoption — Change Management and Culture
item.description: Everything can be built perfectly and still fail, because an unused capability creates nothing. Name the replace-me fear honestly, spread adoption along trust networks — champions, local proof, the pragmatic middle, skeptics given a real role — change the work (metrics, incentives, managers) not just the tools, and measure in layers with the downtime-complaint canary. Closes the series.

item.title: What an AI Production Readiness Audit Actually Covers
item.description: 'Is our AI ready for production?' answered with evidence instead of a feeling: the six dimensions an audit covers — success criteria, evaluation, grounding, cost and latency at volume, security, reliability and ownership — with the red flags for each, and what you walk away with. Useful even if you run it yourself.

item.title: Learning from Experience — Procedural Memory and Agents That Get Better
item.description: Learning without weight changes lands in artifacts: rules, playbooks, worked examples, failure memory. The loop breaks at misattribution, overgeneralization, rot, and conflict — and procedural writes deserve deploy-grade brakes: proposal review, provenance, blast-radius scoping, regression evals. Start with failure memory and worked examples; they compound at a fraction of the risk.

item.title: Preparing Security Teams for AI Adoption
item.description: Security meets AI twice: as shadow AI employees already use, then as the systems the business wants to deploy. Treat shadow AI as demand signal, learn the genuinely new surface — prompts as exfiltration, injection via content, agents as non-human identities, fluent wrongness — and build the paved road with risk-tiered review so the safe path is the fast path.

item.title: Fractional Forward Deployed Engineer vs. Hiring In-House
item.description: Three honest options when your AI initiative needs help: hire in-house (permanence, but months to productive in a thin market), a consultancy (a deliverable whose knowledge walks out), or a fractional forward deployed engineer (the experience gap filled now, with transfer built in). Which fits when — including when you should just hire.

item.title: Memory as Tools — Paging, Files, and Agents That Manage Their Own Minds
item.description: The agentic turn: context as RAM, store as disk, the model participating in paging policy — plus file-based memory as the transparent, diff-reviewable baseline, and consolidation as the background process that extracts facts, distills lessons, and revises standing memory. The consolidator is the highest-privilege writer in the system; review and evaluate it like one.

item.title: Documentation and Knowledge in the AI Era
item.description: Grounded AI makes documentation a runtime dependency: the system's quality ceiling is the corpus's quality, and a stale document becomes a confident wrong answer with a citation. Documentation written to be retrieved, run as a living loop — AI's unanswered questions rank the backlog, AI drafts, humans verify — scoped per use case and compounding across them.

item.title: Why AI Pilots Stall — and What Unsticking One Takes
item.description: Most stalled AI pilots aren't failing for the reason everyone thinks — the model is usually fine. The five causes I actually find: no written bar for done, proof on data the real world doesn't send, under-scoped integration, an unretired stakeholder fear, and no owner. The diagnostic, and what unsticking takes.

item.title: One Step and Sixty Frames — Distillation, Consistency Models, and Video Diffusion
item.description: The step bill falls to one by learning destinations instead of following paths: progressive distillation halves step counts, adversarial losses restore sharpness, consistency models make point-to-endpoint the objective itself. Then video — the same stack over spacetime patches, where temporal coherence is just attention across time. Closes the series with the factored mental model.

item.title: Structured and Graph Memory — When Facts Need Shape
item.description: Similarity search breaks on aggregation, multi-hop, identity, and what-is-true-now. The fix is shape: entity-centric memory with resolved, superseding claims as the 80% answer; knowledge-graph edges (owns, depends_on, supersedes) where relations are the content; and a hybrid end state where the structured layer answers precisely and the episodic store keeps the receipts.

item.title: Scaling AI from Pilot to Enterprise
item.description: Scaling is where most enterprise AI quietly dies — it is a different problem from piloting, and it stands on three legs built while delivering: a platform proven by use case #3 shipping faster than #1, governance written down before scale multiplies risk, and enablement that outlives the first team. Scale by delivering, and watch time-to-ship, not platform size.

item.title: Flow Matching — Straightening the Path from Noise to Image
item.description: If generation is transport from noise to data, why inherit a curved path from a noising process? Flow matching chooses the path — straight — and regresses a network onto its constant velocity: image minus noise. Rectified flow straightens further toward one-step sampling, and CFG, DiT, and latents all carry over unchanged.

item.title: Retrieval Memory — Vector Stores, Scoring, and the Art of Remembering the Right Thing
item.description: Memory retrieval is not document RAG: the store is self-generated, time-sensitive, and self-contradicting. Score on relevance x recency x importance, enforce write-side hygiene — self-contained memories, dedupe at the door, attached structure — and inject under a budget with provenance labels so memories are weighed, not absorbed.

item.title: From Task Automation to Agentic Process Orchestration
item.description: A task is not a process — and the value of most processes lives in the connective tissue between tasks. Agentic systems make that automatable: routing, glue, the routine majority of cases end-to-end. But autonomy is earned on a ladder — suggest, approve, review, bounded autonomy — with escalation designed first and every decision auditable.

item.title: From U-Net to Diffusion Transformer — The Architecture Underneath the Denoiser
item.description: The denoiser was a U-Net — convolutional hourglass, skip connections, interleaved cross-attention — until the Diffusion Transformer re-answered the same requirements generically: patchify the latent, run a standard transformer, condition via adaptive layer norm. The real win is economic: LLM-style scaling curves, inherited infrastructure, and spacetime patches that set up video.

item.title: Conversation Memory and Compaction — Surviving the Long Session
item.description: The strategy ladder — buffer, sliding window, selective eviction, compaction — and why the top rung needs engineering: a preservation contract for what survives verbatim, structured rolling summaries, boundary-triggered timing, and the architectural rule that compaction should demote to episodic storage, never delete.

item.title: AI Readiness — Processes, Data, Systems, Culture
item.description: A good use case pointed at an unready organization still fails — just more expensively. The honest assessment across four pillars: processes mapped as they actually run, data that's reachable and trustworthy, systems that can be integrated with, and a culture that will actually use the thing. The output is a gap list that becomes the roadmap.

item.title: Conditioning and Classifier-Free Guidance — How Text Steers the Image
item.description: Conditioning wires the prompt into every denoising step via text encoders and cross-attention — but the honest conditional distribution follows prompts too loosely. Classifier-free guidance fixes it: co-train an unconditional mode, then extrapolate the difference at sampling. One knob for fidelity vs diversity, 2× cost, and negative prompts for free.

item.title: The Memory Hierarchy of an Agent
item.description: Agent memory decomposes into four types with different jobs: working (the context window), episodic (what happened — read as history), semantic (what is true — needs revision, not just insertion), and procedural (how to act — evolves like code). They differ in storage, retrieval, and lifecycle, and most memory bugs are type confusions.

item.title: Finding High-Value AI Use Cases
item.description: The fastest way to waste an AI budget is to build the wrong thing impressively. Use-case selection as a portfolio: value x feasibility scoring, the signatures of problems suited to AI (and the anti-signatures), resisting AI theater, and sequencing early wins against foundational bets so the program compounds.

item.title: Latent Diffusion — Why Stable Diffusion Doesn't Diffuse Pixels
item.description: Stable Diffusion doesn't diffuse pixels. A perceptually-trained autoencoder compresses images ~48×, the entire diffusion apparatus runs unchanged on latents, and a decoder re-synthesizes texture once at the end. The economics, the three-piece architecture, the autoencoder-as-quality-ceiling caveat, and why video inherited the pattern.

item.title: Why Agents Forget — The Context Window Is Not Memory
item.description: LLMs are stateless, and the context window is working memory — bounded, ephemeral, and unevenly attended — not memory. Forgetting costs re-work, broken user relationships, repeated mistakes, and drift, and no model upgrade fixes it: memory is the system around the model. Opens an 8-post series on building it.

item.title: The Enterprise AI Adoption Problem
item.description: Almost every enterprise has run an AI pilot; far fewer have turned one into value at scale. The gap is mostly organizational, not technical — and crossing it means treating adoption as a repeatable capability, not a series of one-off projects. Opens an 8-post playbook and maps the adoption lifecycle the series walks.

item.title: Sampling Faster — DDIM and the Art of Skipping Steps
item.description: DDPM's thousand steps were a property of one sampler, not the trained network. DDIM's deterministic walk follows the probability flow ODE — 50 steps, zero retraining, plus invertible noise-space addresses — and the sampler zoo is just numerical analysis: a ~40× cost cut from math alone, down to the ~10-step curvature floor.

item.title: The Score-Based View — Gradients, SDEs, and Why Denoising Learns Direction
item.description: The denoiser is secretly learning the score — the gradient of log-probability pointing toward more-plausible images. Langevin dynamics, why denoising and score matching are the same computation, and the continuous limit: a reverse-time SDE and its deterministic twin, the probability flow ODE, where fast sampling and flow matching live.

item.title: From Field Lessons to Better Products
item.description: The most valuable output of an engagement is what you learned shipping it. Captured and fed back, field lessons turn bespoke wins into reusable patterns and better products — the discipline that makes forward deployment compound instead of rotting into a custom-build shop. Lessons, reuse, patterns, product feedback, and the field-to-product flywheel; closes the six-theme field guide.

item.title: Learning to Denoise — DDPM and the Loss That Trains Every Image Model
item.description: Small Gaussian forward steps make each reverse step approximately Gaussian — so generation reduces to regression. DDPM's recipe: predict the added noise, score it with plain mean squared error, sample by walking the chain backwards with fresh noise injected each step. Four lines of training loop, and why they beat the trilemma.

item.title: The FDE Craft: People, Practice & Influence
item.description: Everything technical runs on something human: working with stakeholders, growing in the role, building a team, and shaping a community. The craft and the career — stakeholders, the role and spectrum, careers, hiring, mentoring and coaching, community and influence — plus why the role is exploding at AI companies and builder-communicators are the scarce resource.

item.title: The Forward Process — Destroying Images with Noise, Carefully
item.description: The forward process is a fixed Markov chain that turns any image into pure Gaussian static — no learning anywhere. Why Gaussian noise (closure), what the noise schedule allocates (practice time across corruption levels), the closed-form jump that makes training random-access, and the known endpoint generation starts from.

item.title: Shipping AI: Production, Security & Reliability
item.description: Proving value on a prototype is the halfway point; the harder half is making it survive production — evaluated, secured, compliant, reliable, and owned by the customer's team. Deployment, evaluation, AI security, sovereignty and compliance, reliability, and handover, plus the new AI topics (agent security, operationalized governance, sovereign AI, evals as infrastructure).

item.title: Why Generating Images Is Hard — The Problem Diffusion Solved
item.description: Every text-to-image system rests on one idea: destroy an image with noise, then learn to run the destruction backwards. Why generation is sampling (not prediction), how VAEs blur and GANs collapse, the quality/diversity/stability trilemma — and the iterative-refinement move that escaped it, opening a 10-post series.

item.title: Finding the Right Problem & Proving Value
item.description: You can execute flawlessly on the wrong problem and create nothing. The highest-leverage work is choosing what to build and proving, on real data, that it was worth it: discovery, use-case selection, scope, prototypes and acceptance criteria, and value — plus the AI-era additions (eval-driven scoping, the POC as the crux, value measurement for probabilistic systems).

item.title: From Sales Engineer to Forward Deployed Engineer
item.description: When a demo no longer proves value and the deal is decided in production, the person who wins it is the one who can build the win next to the customer. The technical-GTM spectrum (SE → FDE → CS), why AI made the forward deployed engineer mandatory, the craft tension of scoping and productizing, and how the role becomes a career and a business.

item.title: Building Agents & AI Systems
item.description: The technical heart of the discipline — building agents and AI systems — done the forward-deployed way: on the customer's real data, inside their constraints, with cost and latency first-class. Agents and orchestration, MCP and connectors, context engineering, data and grounding, cost and latency, and the new AI topics (MCP as a standard, agent memory, cost/latency engineering).

item.title: The Technical Win — Proving Value on Real Data
item.description: The technical win is when an AI deal becomes real: documented evidence, on the customer’s data, against an agreed bar, that the feared risk is retired. The four properties of a real AI technical win, proving value (not model accuracy), the double duty of evaluation and guardrails, and how to make the win undeniable and hand it to the people who weren’t in the room.

item.title: Understanding Customers & Driving AI Adoption
item.description: A forward-deployed engineer's first job isn't to build — it's to understand the customer: how they really work, whether they're ready for AI, and what adoption will take. This opens a six-theme field guide to the FDE discipline and covers workflow mapping, AI readiness, adoption as a people problem, and the new AI dynamics (calibrated trust, workflow-native agents, AI maturity).

item.title: The POC Is Where AI Deals Die
item.description: For AI the POC is the crux of the deal — and the most common place AI deals die, almost always from ambiguity, not technical failure. Why AI POCs die, and how to scope one before running it: agree the task, the bar, the data, and the day-after in writing, so the trial becomes a decision procedure that closes.

item.title: Why a Great AI Demo Doesn't Close
item.description: A polished AI demo proves your product can do something impressive once, on data you chose; the buyer needs to know it works reliably on data they didn’t. The demo trap, why AI makes it worse, and how to reframe the demo so it earns a scoped proof on real data instead of standing in for it.

item.title: AI Discovery — Selling Into Fear
item.description: Classic discovery finds a business pain; AI discovery must also surface the fear — hallucination, cost, security, lock-in. The two jobs of AI discovery, the four fears to name out loud, why the best discovery disqualifies, and how to quantify value in the buyer’s terms.

item.title: Why Selling AI Is Different
item.description: The classic technical-sales playbook was written for deterministic software; AI is probabilistic, fails in unfamiliar ways, and a demo proves almost nothing about production. Why selling AI is different — probabilistic behavior, invisible difficulty, a fearful buyer — and why the sale’s center of gravity shifts from the demo to production.

item.title: Helping AI Teams Turn Great Demos into Real Production Value
item.description: I'm opening up my consulting, focused on forward deployed engineering for AI and technical teams. One of the most remarkable things about this moment in AI is how quickly an idea becomes a convincing demo — and the most meaningful work is turning that demo into dependable value inside a customer's real environment. Here's the work I'd love to help with, and why it matters to me.

item.title: The Multiplier Mindset: Consulting That Leaves Teams Stronger
item.description: The best outcome of a consulting engagement isn't that the consultant becomes indispensable — it's that the team no longer needs them. The multiplier mindset — amplifying a team's capability instead of creating dependency — is both the more honorable goal and the better business, and it's the heart of forward-deployed work done well.

item.title: The Long Game — A Career Built on Leaving Teams Stronger
item.description: Any single engagement can be won with cleverness; a career can only be built on a reputation for leaving every team genuinely better off. Reputation as the only durable asset, generosity as a long-term strategy, what stays when the technology changes, and the single standard that lets a career take care of itself.

item.title: Staying Independent — The Sustainable Practice
item.description: Forward-deployed work is intense by nature — you embed, you care, you carry someone else’s deadline as your own — and doing it for years without burning out takes a discipline nobody warns you about. The specific intensity of embedded work, protecting the asset that is you, financial and psychological independence, and variety as renewal.

item.title: From One Win to a Practice — How Referrals Compound
item.description: A consulting practice isn’t built by marketing — it’s built by engagements that go so well the client becomes the source of the next one. Why forward-deployed work refers so well, why the second engagement with the same client is the most valuable pipeline, how to tend the compounding without selling, and the patience it requires.

item.title: The Handoff — Leaving the Team Stronger
item.description: The handoff is the moment of truth for forward-deployed work — everything you did or didn’t do earlier shows up in whether the team can carry the thing forward without you. Why a good handoff starts on day one, handing over understanding rather than just artifacts, and how to engineer your own obsolescence on purpose.

item.title: Building Alongside, Not in a Black Box
item.description: You can deliver the same working system two ways — build it yourself and hand it over, or build it with the team so the capability stays. They look identical on the last day and could not be more different six months later. Why the black box is tempting and costly, what building alongside looks like daily, and how it redefines the deliverable.

item.title: Saying No — The Most Underrated Consulting Skill
item.description: The consultant who says yes to everything looks accommodating and is quietly failing the client. Why the unexamined yes harms — to the wrong engagement, the wrong feature, the wrong architecture — how a well-reasoned no is what makes your yes trustworthy, how to say it well, and the hardest no of all: to work you want but shouldn’t take.

item.title: Earning Trust in the First Two Weeks
item.description: A forward-deployed consultant is a stranger given deep access to a team’s work, and the first two weeks decide whether that stranger becomes someone the team is glad is there. Building trust through small visible usefulness, pairing credibility with warmth, winning over the person who didn’t want you there, and why trust is the real deliverable of the beginning.
